claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.label: Fine internal networks and granules seen in fixed cells are largely artefacts
claims.statement: Fixation preserves the general outward form of small organisms and cells, but the minute internal networks and granules described as the structure of protoplasm are to a large extent artefacts of coagulating fixatives, although larger structures such as nucleus, vacuoles, centrosomes and the spindle are really present in the living cell.

operationalizations.text: Register live-cell images with the same cells or matched samples after chemical fixation and quantify appearance, disappearance, and distortion of fine networks and granules versus larger organelles. A high fraction of fixation-specific fine structures alongside preservation of larger structures supports the claim.

Score fine cytoplasmic networks and granules in chemically fixed cells against the same cells or matched living cells, and separately score nucleus, vacuoles, centrosomes and spindle. Fine texture present in fixed cells and absent in living cells, with the larger organelles retained, would support the claim; the same fine texture in living cells would refute it.

obstacles: Precisely matched live-to-fixed cells are less common than unmatched images.
Modern fixation methods differ from those Thompson criticized.
Not every historical fixative is represented by a correlative live-fixed pair.
Some granules are real and some are precipitates, so a single global fraction is an average over structures.

roles: Public correlative live/fixed microscopy datasets allow direct artifact quantification.
Deposited light and electron microscopy studies spanning living cells and chemical fixation

roles: Reference images of organelles Thompson treats as real, beside fine cytoplasmic texture

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Paired and matched live-cell and fixed-cell image studies of cytoplasmic texture

claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.label: Tree trunk diameter must grow as the 3/2 power of height
claims.statement: For a tree to stand without buckling under its own weight, its diameter must increase as the 3/2 power of its height, which explains why young trees are slender and old large ones stunted, and sets a theoretical maximum tree height (about 300 ft for a Kew-flagstaff pine).

operationalizations.text: Fit log trunk diameter against log height within and across tree species and test whether the slope is 1.5, then evaluate buckling safety factors using wood density and elastic modulus. Strongly different slopes or trees stable beyond the predicted buckling boundary would refute the stated law.

Regress log stem diameter on log height. An exponent near 3/2 would support elastic similarity; exponents near 1 or 2 would favor geometric similarity or constant-stress scaling instead. The separate numerical cap of about 300 ft is checked by inserting the measured taper, density, and modulus of a pine of the Kew-flagstaff form into Greenhill's buckling formula.

obstacles: Diameter and height are not always measured together openly.
Taper, branching, wind loading and species-specific wood properties violate homogeneity.
Inventories are cross-sectional, so young-versus-old slenderness is inferred from size rather than from followed stems.
Wind and hydraulics predict exponents similar to elastic buckling, and elastic modulus is not in the density table.

roles: National forest inventory stem diameters and heights, including small stems, for the same allometric test

candidate_datasets.name: ForestGEO
roles: Long-term tree censuses with stem diameter and species across forest plots.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Wood Density Database
roles: Wood density for thousands of taxa, one material constant in the self-buckling height calculation

candidate_datasets.name: Tallo
roles: Individual tree stem diameter and height for fitting the diameter-height exponent across thousands of species

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
roles: Plant traits including height and wood properties for allometric tests.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Adult human stature declines well before fifty and markedly by old age
claims.statement: Full adult stature in man lasts only for a time: it begins to decrease well before fifty, is notably lessened by sixty, and is much reduced in extreme old age, so that growth takes a negative value.

operationalizations.text: Estimate measured standing height by age in adulthood, preferably longitudinally, and test whether decline begins before 50 and is appreciable by 60 and extreme old age. Stable stature through those ages would refute the timing and magnitude claims.

Compare stature in the same adults from early adulthood to before 50, around 60, and in advanced old age. A loss beginning well before 50 and becoming marked by 60 would support the claim; stable height until advanced old age would refute the stated timing.

obstacles: Cross-sectional age differences include cohort effects.
Posture and vertebral compression affect standing height measurement.
Cross-sectional height-by-age mixes shrinkage with the secular increase in peak height.
Longitudinal series that separate those effects are less directly downloadable than NHANES.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
roles: Public measured adult stature across a wide age range.

candidate_datasets.name: Health and Retirement Study
roles: Public longitudinal aging data including physical measurements for older adults.

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
roles: Cross-sectional measured height by adult age, an open but confounded proxy for individual shrinkage

claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.label: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification
claims.statement: Bacteria and micrococci change shape so much with life stage, circumstances and preparation that their specific identity can seldom be recognised by form, so they have a physiological rather than morphological specificity.

operationalizations.text: Train and validate species classifiers using cell-shape features from bacteria imaged across life stages, growth conditions, and preparation methods, and compare performance with physiological or genomic identifiers. The claim is supported if morphology generalizes poorly across conditions while nonmorphological identity remains stable.

Ask how often cell shape class uniquely identifies a bacterial species, and how much shape of the same strain changes with growth phase, medium and preparation. Low identifiability together with large within-strain shape change would support the claim; shape that stably diagnoses species across conditions would refute it.

obstacles: Repository species labels and imaging protocols may be imbalanced.
Modern high-dimensional morphology may outperform the simple visual criteria Thompson meant.
Most strains carry one curated shape, not a series across life stages and preparations.
Shared rod or coccus shapes show low identifiability even when each species is morphologically stable.
Physiological specificity is a much larger character set than the shape field.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
roles: Public bacterial phenotypic and physiological records provide nonmorphological identity features and morphology metadata.
Strain-level cell shape, size and taxonomy for testing whether form identifies species

roles: Large microscopy datasets can support cross-condition shape classification.

roles: Public bacterial imaging studies and supplements provide labeled morphology under varied conditions.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain
claims.statement: There is no simple and constant relation, holding throughout life, between the size of the whole body and that of organs such as brain, heart and liver; the brain in particular falls from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at twenty-five.

operationalizations.text: Estimate organ-to-body mass or volume ratios across age and test whether ratios remain constant; for brain, compare the ratio at birth and age 25 with the stated approximate fractions. Significant age-dependent allometry supports the central claim, while constant ratios refute it.

Plot brain, heart, and liver mass as fractions of body mass from birth to adult ages. For the human brain, the claim predicts a fall from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at age 25. A ratio that stays constant over that span would refute the claim; the same test applied to heart, liver, lion, and dogfish needs their own series.

obstacles: Combining repositories introduces cohort and measurement differences.
Historical fractions may depend on mass-versus-volume conversion.
MRI volume and autopsy weight are not the same quantity, and body mass is often not in the imaging file.
The lion and dogfish series are not in these human-centered archives.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
roles: Public age-specific body measurements for denominator estimates.

roles: Open young-adult brain imaging for adult brain volumes.

roles: Body mass by age, the denominator of the organ-to-body ratio when brain volume comes from another archive

candidate_datasets.name: NIH Pediatric MRI Data Repository
roles: Public pediatric brain imaging and demographic data for brain-volume growth.

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
roles: Public MRI volumes across ages for estimating human brain size; body mass is often stored separately

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Internal secretions and other substances accelerate growth and alter proportions
claims.statement: Substances inside and outside the organism, such as thyroid and pituitary secretions or iodine compounds, can accelerate growth in a way that changes not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.

operationalizations.text: Compare growth rate, final size, and body-part proportions between hormone or iodine perturbations and matched controls. Support requires accelerated growth accompanied by a statistically detectable allometric or shape change, not size alone.

Compare body size and body-proportion phenotypes of animals in which thyroid, pituitary or growth-hormone pathways are disrupted with matched controls. A change in both scale and proportions would confirm that such substances can alter form; size changes that are pure scaling, or no growth effect at all, would count against the claim as stated.

obstacles: Phenotype measurements and treatment doses are heterogeneous.
The claim combines many substances and animal groups.
The open screen is a mouse knockout panel, so tadpoles, birds and external doses such as iodine are outside it.
Some proportion shifts are secondary to illness rather than a specific growth stimulus.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: Hosts open endocrine and developmental experiments with growth and morphology measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: Gene Expression Omnibus
roles: Public hormone-perturbation studies often include treatment metadata and developmental phenotypes.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Public biological imaging datasets can provide morphology under defined perturbations.

roles: Knockout phenotypes for body weight, length and organ or skeletal measures, including endocrine-pathway genes

claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.label: The pronuclei travel curved paths and meet before reaching the centre of the egg
claims.statement: Given an attraction between the male and female pronuclei and a force drawing them toward the egg centre, their paths lie within the triangle formed by the two bodies and the centre, are curved (convex toward the line joining them) unless they start on a diameter, and the pronuclei meet a little before the centre and then travel straight to it.

operationalizations.text: Segment male and female pronuclei and the egg center in 3D time-lapse fertilization movies, then measure path curvature, convexity, meeting position, and post-meeting trajectory. The stated geometry is confirmed if non-diametric starts produce the predicted curves and precentral meeting consistently; contrary trajectories refute it.

Track male and female pronuclei from sperm entry until they meet, and test three predictions: paths stay inside the triangle they form with the egg centre, curves are convex toward the line joining the pronuclei unless they start on a diameter, and they meet before the centre and only then move straight to it. That geometry would support the claim; straight paths, or a meeting at or beyond the centre, would refute it.

obstacles: Public datasets may emphasize model organisms other than frogs.
Projection of 3D paths into 2D can bias curvature.
Ready-made coordinate tables are rarer than the movies.
Public movies are concentrated on nematode, mouse and echinoderm eggs rather than the frog geometry Thompson illustrated.
Meeting before the centre can arise from more than one force law.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Open fertilization and early-embryo time-lapse microscopy can supply pronuclear trajectories.
Deposited fertilization and early-embryo movies for path geometry

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Public multidimensional embryo imaging supports geometric trajectory analysis.
Embryo time-lapse studies from which pronuclear positions can be tracked in model species

claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.label: A cylindrical cell's end cap has twice the cylinder's radius and height about 0.27R
claims.statement: Where a cylindrical cell of uniform wall tension is capped by part of a sphere, the sphere's radius is twice the cylinder's radius, the cap subtends a cone of 60°, and its height is about 0.27 of the cylinder radius (a little more than one-eighth of the diameter), proportions seen in the free end cells of Spirogyra.

operationalizations.text: Measure cylinder radius, cap curvature radius, subtended angle, and cap height from calibrated 3D or optical images of free-ended Spirogyra cells. The law is supported if ratios cluster near 2 for sphere-to-cylinder radius and 0.27 for cap-height-to-cylinder-radius, with deviations linked to unequal tension.

On free end cells of Spirogyra and similar filaments, measure cylinder radius R and end-cap height, and test the predictions that cap height is about 0.27R and that the cap is a portion of a sphere of radius 2R subtending 60 degrees. A tight cluster around those values would support the claim; a mean far from 0.27R, or a cap radius other than 2R, would refute it.

obstacles: Open Spirogyra samples with calibration and free end cells are limited.
2D orientation biases cap measurements.
Wall anisotropy may violate the uniform-tension premise.
AlgaeBase images are illustrations, not a random sample of free end cells.
Turgor and wall thickness are not recorded with the photographs.
The numerical target assumes uniform wall tension, which may vary along the filament.

candidate_datasets.name: AlgaeBase
roles: Taxonomic images of Spirogyra and other filamentous algae from which end-cap proportions can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Microscopy datasets can supply higher-resolution or 3D filamentous-alga measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
roles: Public calibrated algal cell images may provide end-cap geometry.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth
claims.statement: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).

operationalizations.text: Decompose adult size across species into fitted growth rate and duration parameters, then test whether both independently explain final size and whether rabbit–guinea-pig and human–rabbit contrasts follow the stated components. Failure of either component to predict size would refute that part.

Decompose adult size into a rate parameter and a duration for human, rabbit, and guinea pig, and then across mammals more generally. The named contrasts predict a higher rate for the rabbit than the guinea pig and a longer duration for the human than the rabbit. A model that uses only rate or only duration should fail if both factors matter.

obstacles: Databases contain endpoints more often than complete growth trajectories.
Growth rate and duration estimates are statistically correlated.
Phylogeny and ecology confound three-species comparisons.
Energy-budget parameters already impose a rate-duration decomposition, so they are not a fully independent test.
Nutrition in the classical laboratory comparisons is not standardized across species.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge
roles: Public mammalian development, maturity, adult mass and longevity traits.
Adult body mass and longevity as coarse correlates of size and growth duration

roles: Growth data and life-cycle parameters for human, rabbit, guinea pig, and many other mammals

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction
claims.statement: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).

operationalizations.text: Fit growth or development rates across temperatures within normal ranges and calculate Q10 values, testing whether rates rise approximately exponentially and Q10 commonly lies between two and three. Systematic non-exponential responses or Q10 values outside that range would refute the stated law.

Below the optimum, compute the factor by which growth rate changes per 10°C. A factor of about 2 to 3, the same order as ordinary chemical reactions, would support the claim. A factor near 1 across the normal range, or systematically an order of magnitude larger, would refute the stated similarity. Intervals above the optimum are outside the qualified claim.

obstacles: Relevant experiments require compilation from many deposits.
Q10 varies with temperature interval and proximity to thermal limits.
Field time series confound temperature with season.
The coefficient itself falls as the temperature interval rises, so the test range has to be declared.
Fitted temperature parameters are not the same object as a raw rate ratio, and tabulated Q10 values are a sparse sample.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
roles: Temperature-correction parameters fitted to growth and development for many animals

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
roles: Published Q10 and rate values for growth and related physiological processes

candidate_datasets.name: BioTIME
roles: Open ecological time-series data with abundance and environmental context for selected temperature-related growth analyses.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: Public experimental datasets containing organismal growth and development across temperatures.

claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.label: Cells of each kind vary little about a mean size, whatever the body size
claims.statement: Cells of each kind vary little about a characteristic mean size and have absolute size limits, so dwarf and giant individuals of a species (e.g. Crepidula, sea-urchin larvae) differ in cell number rather than cell size.

operationalizations.text: Measure volumes of matched cell types across dwarf, normal and giant individuals and regress cell size and cell number on body size. Nearly invariant cell size with number accounting for body-size differences supports the claim; strong within-type cell-size scaling refutes it.

For each cell type, compare the spread of cell size with the spread of body size across dwarf and giant individuals or related species, and partition the body-size difference into cell size versus cell number. The claim is confirmed if cell size stays in a narrow band and cell number accounts for body size; it is refuted if homologous cells scale up with the body.

obstacles: Matched body-size phenotypes and cell types are uncommon in one dataset.
Cell volume estimates depend on tissue preparation and segmentation.
Some tissues vary by ploidy or hypertrophy.
Public sizes are dense for a few tissues and model species, not for the Crepidula and urchin cases named.
Polyploid and hypertrophic tissues are real exceptions and have to be separated by cell class.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Public comparative microscopy datasets with cellular resolution.

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
roles: Published cell sizes and counts for comparing within-type variation with body size

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
roles: Open tissue microscopy for measuring cell dimensions across tissue types.

roles: Microscopy datasets from which cell size distributions can be measured in model tissues

claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.label: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller
claims.statement: Because a micrococcus 0.15 µm across contains only some tens of thousands of protein molecules, the smallest known organisms approach molecular dimensions, and organisms cannot be subdivided indefinitely or be much smaller than those already discovered.

operationalizations.text: Compile verified dimensions, genome sizes and molecular inventories of the smallest free-living and host-dependent organisms, estimate the minimum components required for autonomous life, and compare discovered cells with that bound. Organisms substantially below the proposed scale would refute the historical prediction.

Compare the lower tail of free-living cell diameter with the volume of a minimal genome plus ribosomes. The claim is supported if that tail sits near the packing floor corresponding to tens of thousands of proteins; it is weakened if diverse free-living organisms are far smaller than that floor allows.

obstacles: Reported ultramicrobe sizes can reflect filtration artifacts or nonliving particles.
Dependence on hosts blurs the definition of organism and minimum autonomous machinery.
Culture collections miss many of the smallest uncultured cells.
Where an object stops being an organism and becomes a virus is a definitional boundary at the lower limit.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
roles: Public bacterial and archaeal phenotypes, including cell morphology and dimensions for many strains.
Strain-level bacterial cell dimensions for the observed lower end of organism size

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
roles: Ribosome, protein, and genome-related sizes used to compute a molecular packing floor

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Genome
roles: Public genome assemblies and sizes for microorganisms.

claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell
claims.label: The nucleus is spherical because it is an immiscible fluid drop under uniform tension
claims.statement: The nucleus is almost always spherical because its fluid substance does not mix with the surrounding protoplasm, so it is bounded by a film of uniform surface tension and immersed in a medium transmitting uniform fluid pressure; where the cytoplasm becomes more solid (as in muscle cells or mucus-laden epithelial cells) the pressure becomes unsymmetrical and the nucleus is deformed.

operationalizations.text: Measure nuclear sphericity, cytoplasmic rheology, external stress anisotropy, and nuclear-envelope tension across cell types and perturbations. Support requires round nuclei in fluid isotropic surroundings and predictable deformation as surrounding stiffness or pressure anisotropy increases.

Measure nuclear roundness against cytoplasmic stiffness or solidity across cell types, including muscle and secretory epithelia. Nuclei that are spherical in fluid cytoplasm and systematically deformed where the cytoplasm is stiffened would support the claim; spherical nuclei inside stiffened cytoplasm, or deformed nuclei in uniform fluid cytoplasm, would refute the pressure account.

obstacles: Most image datasets lack matched cytoplasmic rheology or pressure.
Nuclear lamina and chromatin mechanics provide plausible alternative causes.
Image archives rarely include a stiffness measurement for the same cell.
The nuclear lamina and chromatin packing deform nuclei without a change in cytoplasmic fluidity.
Roundness is compatible with an interfacial film and with a tense cortical shell.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Cell-painting and perturbation images provide large-scale nuclear shape measurements.
Cell-image studies in which nuclear outline can be scored against cell type and cytoskeletal state

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
roles: Reference micrographs of resting nuclei in soft and structurally specialised cells

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
roles: Subcellular images of nuclear shape across many human cell types

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas
roles: Public microscopy across cell lines supports comparisons of nuclear shape and cytoskeletal context.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Growth rate is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, metamorphosis
claims.statement: Curves of growth show well-marked interruptions or changes of rate at physiological epochs such as birth and puberty, in man and in other animals, and most strikingly in animals that undergo a regular metamorphosis.

operationalizations.text: Fit segmented growth curves around independently dated birth, puberty and metamorphic transitions and test for discontinuities or slope changes. Smooth trajectories through those epochs would refute the corresponding component.

Test for a change in the slope of growth rate at birth and at puberty in humans, and at metamorphosis in insects, amphibians, and other transforming animals. Marked slope changes at those epochs, strongest where metamorphosis is regular, would support the claim; smooth velocity through them would count against it.

obstacles: Puberty and metamorphosis timing must be measured independently of growth.
Comparable longitudinal mass or size series are sparse outside model species.
Human birth and puberty effects are modest and easy to confuse with a change of environment or measurement.
Metamorphic growth series are not gathered as a single designed dataset.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
roles: Life-cycle trajectories for species with metamorphosis, including some amphibians and insects

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Developmental imaging series that include metamorphic or embryonic transitions in selected animals.

candidate_datasets.name: CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
roles: Human anthropometry around childhood and puberty.

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
roles: Human stature velocity around puberty; birth is only the left edge of the postnatal series

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water
claims.statement: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.

operationalizations.text: Measure abdomen-to-cephalothorax length in Artemia raised or sampled across salinity gradients and fit the ratio as a function of salinity while controlling species, sex, age, and population. A consistently positive salinity effect supports the claim; no effect or a negative effect refutes it.

Regress the abdomen-to-cephalothorax length ratio of Artemia on salinity, holding temperature and food as covariates and comparing populations raised across a salinity series. A positive slope, with named 'species' falling on successive parts of one curve, would support the claim; a flat or negative slope after those controls would refute it.

obstacles: Morphometric data paired with exact salinity are scattered.
Genetic differentiation and age can confound environmental plasticity.
Morphometrics sit in paper tables rather than one open archive.
Wild samples confound salinity with temperature, food and clonal lineage.
Thompson's own isotonic-versus-equal-density test is still not a standard column in those tables.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: Public Artemia salinity experiments and morphometric supplements may provide measurements for a compiled test.

candidate_datasets.name: Zenodo
roles: Open experimental and imaging datasets can supplement Artemia morphology-by-salinity records.

claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.label: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall
claims.statement: A cylindrical cell such as Spirogyra that grows without external restraint takes its form because its developing membrane is anisotropic, extending more easily in one direction; a slight inequality of tension in two directions gives an ellipsoidal cell and a great inequality a cylindrical one.

operationalizations.text: Measure directional wall extensibility and cell aspect ratio in freely growing walled cells, perturb wall anisotropy, and fit a mechanical growth model. Support requires anisotropy to precede and quantitatively predict ellipsoidal-to-cylindrical elongation, with isotropization producing rounder cells.

Measure wall anisotropy, for example cellulose microfibril orientation, against axial versus radial extension in freely grown cylindrical cells, and compare isotropic-wall mutants or treatments. Cylinders where extension is easier along the axis, and a shift toward spheres when anisotropy is lost, would support the claim; cylinders with isotropic walls, or no shape change when anisotropy is removed, would refute it.

obstacles: Direct wall extensibility is rarely measured with morphology.
Turgor and cytoskeletal orientation covary with wall anisotropy.
Spirogyra-specific perturbation data are limited.
Microfibril angle and growth anisotropy are published for model cells, not archived with the algal images.
External constraint is hard to rule out for cells inside a filament.
Turgor pressure is a necessary partner of wall anisotropy, so the wall is not the sole variable.

candidate_datasets.name: AlgaeBase
roles: Images of Spirogyra and other free filaments for the cylindrical form, not for wall-polymer orientation

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Live plant and algal cell-wall imaging can quantify anisotropic growth.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Public morphology perturbation screens can test links between wall machinery and elongation.

claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.label: Viscid spider-thread coating breaks into beads at the cylinder stability limit
claims.statement: The sticky fluid coating of a spider's spiral thread, being a liquid cylinder, becomes unstable when its length exceeds its circumference and breaks up into equal, equally spaced beads (often with smaller beads between), the spacing being somewhat greater than theory owing to viscosity and drag on the core thread.

operationalizations.text: From calibrated orb-web images, measure coating radius, instability wavelength, bead spacing and size hierarchy, then compare them with Rayleigh-Plateau predictions for a viscous coating on a fiber. Support requires onset near the stated circumference criterion and systematic spacing shifts predicted by viscosity and core drag.

On viscid spider capture threads, measure coating radius, bead spacing and bead-size alternation, and compare spacing with the circumference instability threshold and the Rayleigh wavelength. Spacing a little longer than the inviscid prediction, with equal primary beads, would support the claim; a spacing unrelated to cylinder radius, or beads that do not form at that threshold, would refute it.

obstacles: Public images may omit fluid radius, viscosity, or time of formation.
Spider chemistry and active spinning introduce additional controls.
Micrographs are concentrated on a few orb-weaver species and often illustrate rather than sample the thread.
The axial fibre and glue viscosity both shift the ideal wavelength.
No public morphometric table of bead spacing exists.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: Public spider-silk studies may include calibrated microscopy and material measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: Zenodo
roles: Open microscopy and supplementary datasets can add bead-spacing measurements.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time
claims.statement: After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.

operationalizations.text: Derive regenerative tail length or volume velocity from time-lapse measurements after its early maximum and fit a power law V proportional to T raised to negative alpha. The claim is supported if alpha is near 2 and V times T squared is approximately constant, compared with alternative decay models.

After the early maximum, regress log regenerative velocity of tadpole tails on log time since amputation and test whether the slope is −2, equivalently whether velocity times time squared is constant. A slope near −2 would support the claim; a slope near −1, or an exponential decline that fits better, would refute it.

obstacles: Few public series have dense enough time sampling to estimate velocity.
Species, temperature, and injury extent affect the exponent.
Length-versus-time series are in individual papers, not a shared archive.
The first day or two after amputation is often unmeasured, which is where the maximum sits.
Thompson offered the square law for one tadpole series and only guessed it might be general.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Public developmental imaging studies may contain time-resolved tadpole tail-regeneration series.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: Hosts regeneration-study measurements and image supplements suitable for reanalysis.

claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.label: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes
claims.statement: A bud appears on a yeast cell because the surface tension diminishes at one part of the cell surface, so that this area expands, after which the bud's own surface tension rounds it into a roughly spherical form.

operationalizations.text: Measure local membrane or wall tension before and during yeast bud emergence and perturb tension locally while imaging polarity markers. Support requires a local tension drop preceding and inducing expansion, followed by tension-dependent rounding; polarity-driven growth without the predicted drop refutes it.

At the future bud site on a yeast cell, measure local surface tension through bud emergence and test whether a local drop precedes expansion, as against a polarity landmark that directs growth at constant tension. A tension drop that is necessary and sufficient for the bud would support the claim; budding at a marked site with no tension drop, or failure of budding when tension is locally reduced away from the landmark, would refute it.

obstacles: Direct local tension reporters are uncommon in archived yeast data.
Cell-wall remodeling and polarized actin are strong alternative mechanisms.
Phenotype databases record shape and gene, not local tension.
Turgor-driven expansion and a tension drop make similar early bulges.

The claim is favored if required power grows near the 3.5 power of length while muscle power grows near the cube, and weakened if measured flight cost scales no faster than muscle capacity.

Bird proportions and flight styles are not fixed across size.
External morphology does not contain muscle mass or measured flight power.
Real birds change proportions with size, so a mismatch can be read as a failed prediction or as a departure from the premise.

Extant ratites' reduced wings reflect evolutionary history as well as size.
Moa mass and wing reduction are fossil estimates with wide error.
Flightlessness also evolves in birds far below any aerodynamic ceiling.
The ostrich clause is explicitly probable rather than certain.

claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

Shape datasets rarely include all relevant forces.
Taxonomic and scale effects are confounded.
Shape class is not a fit residual to a surface-tension surface.
Walls and skeletons change with size along with the surface-to-volume ratio.
The three archives do not share a common morphometric protocol.

Many images are 2D projections.
A threshold for classifying approximate surface families is needed.
Bacterial vocabularies collapse unduloids into rods or spirals.
Protist coverage in open shape tables is much thinner than bacterial coverage.
Transitions during growth need time series, which these archives mostly lack.

Jump height against size, from small jumpers to large mammals, is scattered through papers rather than held in one public dataset.

Species sampling is concentrated in model organisms.
Phylogenetic relatedness itself induces nonindependence.
Cleavage mode and yolk class are not in a single open table and must be compiled.
Older classifications sometimes used the same embryological characters, so agreement can be partly by construction unless the tree is molecular.
The claim covers animals from segmentation onward, a wider span than any one compiled matrix.

Molecular-force dominance is not implied by low diversity alone.
Shape fields are coarse categories, so 'limited' depends on the coding scheme.
A short list of forms can be phylogenetic conservatism rather than molecular-force control.
Protozoa are poorly represented next to bacteria.

operationalizations.text: Estimate effective viscosity and viscoelastic relaxation from time-resolved amoeba deformation under known pressure or force, and compare flow and relaxation with water and high-viscosity reference fluids. Images are anecdotal relative to a survey of naked cells.

claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude
claims.label: Larger fish can sprint faster but cover similar distances and tire more slowly
claims.statement: Since muscular work available scales as the cube of linear size while the rate of energy supply, depending on respiratory surface, scales only as the square, a larger fish should achieve a much higher burst speed than a smaller one but travel a similar distance over a year, and smaller individuals should fatigue faster and have less staying power.

operationalizations.text: Within closely related fishes, regress burst speed, fatigue time and annual movement distance on body length while controlling temperature and ecology, and compare exponents with the square-cube predictions. Larger fish lacking higher burst speed, or annual distance increasing strongly with size, would refute components of the claim.

Within similar fish, fit burst speed, distance covered over a year, and time to fatigue against length. The claim predicts a steep rise of burst speed with length, little change in annual distance, and faster fatigue in smaller fish; a flat burst speed or an annual distance that scales like burst speed would count against it.

obstacles: Burst speed and fatigue are rarely paired with annual tracking in the same individuals.
Temperature, swimming mode and tag effects confound size comparisons.
Sprint tests, fatigue curves, and annual tracks are rarely available for the same size series.
Reynolds number, temperature, and body shape change with size and can mimic the predicted exponents.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
roles: Body size, ecology and some swimming-related species information.
Body lengths and scattered species-level swimming speeds, not size series of sprint versus endurance

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
roles: Public animal tracking studies that can estimate movement speed and annual distance for selected fishes.
Animal movement tracks, including some fishes, for distance traveled; burst speed and fatigue are not in the tracks

claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.label: Decapod sperm-cell shape is an intermediate phase of osmotic shrinkage
claims.statement: The normal form of decapod crustacean sperm-cells is one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage from a spherical form, caused by osmotic withdrawal of fluid without a matching reduction of surface area, so that equivalent shapes are produced by salt solutions of equivalent (molecular-weight-proportional) concentration.

operationalizations.text: Order decapod sperm shapes along measured osmotic concentration series and test whether volume loss at nearly constant surface area reproduces normal forms and collapses by solute molarity.

Place decapod sperm in a graded osmotic series and in equiosmolar salts of different molecular weight, and record the shape sequence from the sphere. Support would be a single shrinkage pathway ordered by osmolarity, with matching shapes at molecular-weight-proportional concentrations; stable species-specific shapes across that series would refute the claim.

obstacles: Public images rarely include controlled osmolarity metadata.
Species coverage for decapod sperm is limited.
No public osmotic series exists for the named genera Inachus, Galathea, Dromia and crayfish.
Isolated micrographs of crustacean sperm lack the paired external concentration and surface-area measurements the test needs.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
roles: Public microscopy database that can provide some comparative sperm-cell morphology.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Form changes follow the same route in individual development and racial history
claims.statement: Changes of form produced by varying rates of growth are the same phenomenon in individual development and in the differences between species; a transformation from one form to another follows the same course whether it happens within a lifetime or over ancestral history, which accounts for much of von Baer's law of recapitulation.

operationalizations.text: Represent ontogenetic and phylogenetic shape changes in a common morphometric space and compare their trajectories, directions, and ordering of landmarks. Support requires phylogenetic transformations to follow the same paths as within-individual development more often than null or alternative developmental models predict.

In a shape space, compare the trajectory of an ontogenetic series with the trajectory connecting the same forms along a phylogeny. A shared path, within a stated tolerance, would support one road of transformation; ontogenies that bend away from the phylogenetic path would refute it.

obstacles: Ancestral forms must be inferred rather than observed.
Heterochrony can mimic shared paths.
The universal 'one road' formulation is much broader than available clade datasets.
Most scans are adults, so ontogenetic series have to be assembled clade by clade.
Shared allometry can make ontogeny and phylogeny look alike in a low-dimensional shape space.
Coverage is strong for a few vertebrate groups and weak for the stated scope of organic form.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
roles: Open 3D specimens across ages and species support shared-space geometric morphometrics.
3D specimen scans from which ontogenetic and adult shape series can be measured for selected clades

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
roles: Public morphological matrices and images can link comparative form with phylogeny.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
roles: Phylogenetic backbone for ordering species-level shape differences

claims.chapter: Ch. I: Introductory
claims.label: Surface tension at a cell's boundary strongly affects its form
claims.statement: Like other fluid bodies, the surface of a cell such as an Amoeba carries a surface tension that depends on the substance it touches, and this surface tension strongly affects the cell's form.

operationalizations.text: Measure amoeboid cell boundary curvature and shape as the contacting medium changes, estimate cortical or interfacial tension, and test whether tension predicts the deformation after controlling for active cytoskeletal forces. A reproducible medium-dependent tension-shape relation would support the claim.

Treat cortical tension as the modern stand-in for Thompson's interfacial tension, then relate measured boundary stress in amoeboid cells to outline curvature. The claim is favored if lowering that stress produces the protrusions and loss of rounding it requires, and weakened if shape is indifferent to boundary stress.

obstacles: Historical surface tension maps imperfectly to active cortical tension.
Most image datasets lack independent force measurements.
Cortical tension is an active regulated stress, not the passive surface tension of a fluid interface.
Paired tension-and-shape series sit in paper supplements rather than in the image archives.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
roles: Public microscopy of cells, including amoeboid forms, for boundary-shape measurements.
Cell-shape images, including free-living amoebae, for morphometry of the fluid outline

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Public microscopy datasets that may pair perturbations with cell-shape dynamics.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
roles: Public cell-imaging studies with outlines of amoeboid and other cells; tension itself is usually not in the archive

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Regeneration is ordinary growth, with the same curve as growth from zero
claims.statement: Regeneration is a particular case of growth obeying the same laws; the regeneration curve (short latent period, rapid rise to a maximum velocity, then slow decline) only appears different because ordinary growth curves start at birth, and a complete growth curve from zero has the same essential features.

operationalizations.text: Normalize complete regeneration and whole-organism growth trajectories and compare their latent, accelerating, peak-velocity, and decelerating phases using shared versus separate curve families. Support requires a common curve structure across matched tissues or taxa; systematic phase or shape differences refute it.

Align regeneration curves and whole-organism growth curves on a common time origin at the start of growth, and compare the sequence latent period, rise to a velocity maximum, then slow decline. Matching sequence and comparable scaled shape would support the claim; a regeneration curve that stays monotonic, or a full growth curve that lacks the rising limb, would refute a shared shape.

obstacles: 'Same essential characteristics' permits multiple interpretations.
Matched regeneration and zero-origin ontogeny data are rare.
Normalization can conceal biologically important differences.
Regeneration lengths are scattered across papers and start after a latent period that is poorly sampled.
Many unrelated processes share a rise-and-fall velocity curve.
'Essential features' does not specify a numerical tolerance.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
roles: Whole-organism size-at-age curves, the ordinary-growth side of a comparison with regeneration time series

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Time-lapse regeneration and development images can yield comparable growth trajectories.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: Open regeneration and ontogenetic-growth datasets can be assembled for model comparison.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends
claims.statement: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.

operationalizations.text: Estimate organ-specific growth trajectories and test whether their relative rates predict species- or genotype-specific adult morphology. Perturbations or natural variants that change local rates and produce the predicted form differences would support causality; unchanged morphology would refute it in that system.

Estimate a specific growth rate for the whole body and for separate organs, then ask how much adult shape difference those local rate differences produce. The claim is favored if small, persistent rate differences account for a large share of between-species form; it is hard to refute, because no share is named as too small.

obstacles: Specific morphology and large part lack quantitative thresholds.
Local growth can be consequence as well as cause of patterning.
Comparable trajectories across taxa are sparse.
Organ-specific growth rates are published piecemeal.
A very large part of specific morphology does not state how large a part would fail the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
roles: Whole-organism growth rates across species; organ-specific rates are not the main content

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
roles: Time-resolved organism and organ development images for local growth estimates.

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
roles: Scattered organ and body sizes at different stages, from which crude local growth can sometimes be inferred

candidate_datasets.name: e-Mouse Atlas Project
roles: Stage-resolved 3D mouse anatomy for organ-specific growth trajectories.

claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth
claims.label: Claw reversal after amputation depends on regeneration versus growth rates
claims.statement: Whether an amputated large crustacean claw regenerates as the large claw, or the claws exchange roles, depends on the ratio between the regenerative growth rate of the amputated claw and the growth rate of the uninjured claw, since claw form follows claw size.

operationalizations.text: For individually tracked asymmetric-clawed crustaceans, estimate post-amputation growth rates of both claws and test whether their ratio predicts retention versus reversal of claw identity and morphology. A threshold relationship that predicts outcomes independently of species and body size would support the mechanism.

After claw amputation, measure the regenerative growth rate of the stump and the growth rate of the intact claw, and predict reversal from whether the intact claw reaches the large-claw size class first. Reversal when and only when that ratio favours the intact claw would support the claim; reversal uncorrelated with the two rates would refute it.

obstacles: The required individual-level bilateral growth trajectories are rarely archived.
Neural and positional effects could confound a rate-only explanation.
Paired rate measurements are spread across lobster, snapping-shrimp and crab papers.
Nerve supply, molt stage and a handedness program can reverse claws at the same sizes.
Form-follows-size has to be granted before the rate ratio is interpreted.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
roles: May contain public crustacean regeneration experiments, though matched bilateral time series are sparse.

claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells
claims.label: Elastic fibrillae act as a microscopic skeleton shaping spiral cells
claims.statement: The spiral and other peculiar forms of decapod sperm-cells and of many Infusoria are produced by more or less elastic fibrillae in the cell, which restrain and modify the surface forces like the wire frames and coils in Plateau's experiments, acting as a microscopic skeleton.

operationalizations.text: Co-register cell shape with internal fibril ultrastructure and test whether fibril position, orientation, and elasticity predict spiral form better than membrane forces alone.

Map intracellular fibrils onto the spiral or other non-equilibrium outline of decapod sperm and ciliates, and ask whether the outline relaxes when those fibrils are absent. A fibrillar scaffold whose geometry matches the departure from a surface-tension figure would support the claim; the same outlines without such fibrils, or fibrils that do not follow the spiral, would weaken it.

obstacles: Elasticity is not inferable reliably from fixed ultrastructure.
Sparse taxonomic coverage limits the broad generalization.
Cortex and sperm ultrastructure are spread across individual papers, with quantitative shape-versus-fibril tables for only a few model ciliates.
Nearly all of these cells have a cytoskeleton, so presence alone does not show that the fibrils act as Plateau frames.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
roles: Comparative public cell imagery for infusorian and sperm morphology.

candidate_datasets.name: EMPIAR
roles: Open volume electron-microscopy data for relating cytoskeletal fibrils to whole-cell form.
